cards.html:
1 · Rebase with conflicts. You resolve once per replayed commit that touches the conflicting line: if both feature commits change features:, twice. git reflog shows an entry like rebase (start); the line before it is your old tip: git reset --hard HEAD@{n} with that n (right after the rebase, git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD does the same).

2 · Clean history. git commit --fixup <sha> creates fixup! <message>; git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main pre-sorts it under its target with the fixup command; then reword the remaining commits to feat: … / test: ….

3 · The force-push trap. After git fetch the lease matches the remote, so --force-with-lease overwrites the colleague's commit; their git pull --rebase then drops it locally as well. They recover it with git reflog (the commit: line) and git cherry-pick <sha>. With --force-if-includes the push is rejected with (remote ref updated since checkout), because the remote tip was never part of your local history.

4 · Lock file conflict. Edit pyproject.toml to keep both dependencies, then git checkout --theirs uv.lock, uv lock, git add pyproject.toml uv.lock, uv sync --locked (must succeed), git commit. Hand-editing uv.lock is never the answer.

5 · Semantic conflict. Both merges succeed; pytest on main fails with an ImportError. "Require branches to be up to date before merging" would have forced the second PR to include the first and re-run CI, which fails. The cost: every merge invalidates the other open PRs' checks, so busy teams spend time re-running CI, which is the problem a merge queue solves.

6 · Schema test.

@pytest.mark.parametrize("field, value", [
    ("credit_amount", -1), ("duration", 200), ("purpose", None)])
def test_invalid_requests(client, applicant, field, value):
    if value is None:
        del applicant[field]
    else:
        applicant[field] = value
    assert client.post("/predict", json=applicant).status_code == 422

7 · Schedule. Add under on:: schedule: [{cron: "0 4 * * *"}] and workflow_dispatch:.

8 · Find the order dependence. We ran it: the full suite gives 1 failed, 26 passed; the failure is test_real_data_passes_contract with pandera's in_range(18, 100) check on age. uv run pytest tests/test_data.py alone gives 9 passed. pytest runs files in alphabetical order, so test_api.py mutates the session-scoped df before test_data.py uses it. Fix: df = df.copy() in the new test.

9 · The pipe trap. Without shell:, the step runs with bash -e, and the pipeline's exit code is tee's (0): green. With defaults: run: shell: bash it runs with -o pipefail, so pytest's exit code 1 fails the step.

10 · OS dimension. matrix: {python-version: ["3.12", "3.13"], os: [ubuntu-latest]} plus include: [{python-version: "3.12", os: macos-latest}] gives three jobs; use runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}. On private repositories macOS minutes are billed at a higher rate than Linux minutes.

11 · Protect yourself. The PR shows "Merging is blocked" and the failing required check (ci-ok, because lint failed).

12 · Prove the aggregator. (a) The matrix jobs get new names, but ci-ok still runs and reports, so the PR can be merged. (b) Without if: always(), ci-ok is skipped when test fails, and GitHub treats a skipped required check as passing: a PR with failing tests becomes mergeable. That is why the condition is essential.

13 · Read the linters. Sort the imports and delete import os; cols: list[str] | None = None with for c in cols or []:; except Exception as err: raise ValueError(...) from err; type hints for load(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame. The fix that changes behaviour is threshold: it needs a final branch, e.g. raise ValueError(f"unknown threshold {name!r}"), so an unknown name now fails loudly instead of returning None.

14 · Approval gate. Approve via Review deployments; roll back with Rollback → Run workflow and the previous SHA (find it in the run history or with aws ecr describe-images); curl <url>/health shows the old version.

15 · Prove the environment rule. GitHub refuses to start the job before any step runs, with a message that the branch is not allowed to deploy to staging because of the environment's protection rules; no OIDC token is issued, so AWS is never asked. With all branches allowed, the staging role accepts the token (sub = …:environment:staging) and get-caller-identity prints the staging role. That is still not a production risk: the staging role can only update credit-api-staging. Defence in depth: either control alone blocks the attack on production.

16 · Break OIDC on purpose. With environment: staging the login fails with Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity: the sub becomes …:environment:staging, but the build role trusts only …:ref:refs/heads/main. (With the single role of the previous edition it would have worked, which was part of the problem.) With a job-level permissions: {contents: read} the job loses id-token: write, because job permissions replace the workflow's, and the step fails with Credentials could not be loaded.

17 · Listen-address bug. From the host, curl fails (typically Connection reset by peer or Empty reply from server); from inside the container, the same request succeeds. That proves the app is running but only reachable on the container's own loopback interface.

18 · Break the data. The test job fails first, in test_real_data_passes_contract, with a pandera SchemaErrors report naming column age, check in_range(18, 100) and the row index; the model gate never runs because it needs: test.

19 · Worse retrieval. One chunk per document makes chunks long and diluted, so several documents look similar and ranks get worse: MRR drops. With k=1 (after adding a hit_rate_at_1 threshold), the hit rate equals the share of first-place hits: in our run 19 of 20 questions had the right document first, so 0.95.

20 · Paired promotion. The core of the new promote.py:

champ = mlflow.sklearn.load_model(f"models:/{NAME}@champion")
chall = mlflow.sklearn.load_model(f"models:/{NAME}/{newest.version}")
_, x_test, _, y_test = current_split()      # same rows for both
base = {"roc_auc": auc(champ, x_test, y_test)}
new = {"roc_auc": auc(chall, x_test, y_test)}
failures = check(new, base, cfg["floors"], cfg["max_drop"])

current_split() reuses the exact train_test_split call from train.py (move it into a function so both use one definition).

21 · A slice gate. In train(), after computing proba: young = x_test["age"] < 25 and metrics["roc_auc_age_lt_25"] = roc_auc_score(y_test[young], proba[young]). check() loops over floors, so adding the floor is enough; baseline.get() returns 0 for a missing baseline value, so the first run passes the drop check. If the slice contains only one class, roc_auc_score raises ValueError; guard it (skip the metric and print a warning when y_test[young].nunique() < 2 or the slice has fewer than, say, 30 rows) and make the gate treat a missing slice metric as "not checked" rather than as 0.

22 · Fix the cache key.

payload = {"model": self.model, "prompt": prompt,
           "max_tokens": self.max_tokens}
key = hashlib.sha256(
    json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()

The test creates two generators with different max_tokens, a fake client that returns a fixed text, and a tmp_path cache directory; after one call each, len(list(tmp_path.iterdir())) == 2.

23 · Your first alarm. Without a model file, /predict and /health return 503, which the filter $.status >= 500 counts. The quickest way in staging: deploy an image with a wrong MODEL_PATH environment variable (the deployment will fail its health checks, which is also a valid test of the alarm on the old tasks being replaced; watch both). The runbook entry names the alarm, its meaning, the first three commands and the rollback.

24 · Budget arithmetic. 30 days × 24 h × 60 min × 0.001 = 43.2 minutes of full outage. Four minutes at 50 % errors equal two minutes of full outage, so the deployment used about 2 / 43.2 ≈ 4.6 % of the month's budget.

25 · Run the game day. The local run reproduces the output in Section 7.5. A good postmortem lists the timeline (10:40 merge, 10:47 staging check failed or, in the hypothetical, production impact until 11:20), impact (33 minutes of approving every applicant), root cause (threshold default changed in code), contributing factors (business parameter without owner or test; no decision-level check before this chapter), and action items: move the threshold to thresholds.json under CODEOWNERS (prevent), distribution check in every deploy (detect), rollback rehearsal (mitigate).

26 · Rewrite a junior answer. For example: "Every PR runs lint, types and tests on two Python versions. The interesting part is the model gate: I measured that the train/test split alone moves AUC by ±0.025, so a fixed 0.03 tolerance only works with a fixed split; I made the split part of the data contract. My first version also had a security hole in the deploy role, which a review found…"

27 · Mock system design. Check your recording for: the clarifying questions (how often prompts change, who edits them, cost budget, regulated data?), prompts in Git, deterministic hard gates vs. advisory LLM judging on PRs, cost controls with a complete cache key, prompt version in logs, a feature-flag rollout, a held-out set, and the model version pinned.

28 · Fill the Measured table. gh run list --workflow ci.yml --limit 5 --json createdAt,updatedAt gives start and end times; take the median. For merge-to-production, subtract the approval wait shown on the run page. For rollback, time from clicking Run workflow to /health reporting the old SHA.
